prompt: An ALB target group has three registered targets. One target's database connection pool is exhausted, so its /health endpoint starts returning 503, while the other two targets are fine. With unhealthy_threshold = 3 and interval = 15, what happens?
choices: The entire target group is marked unhealthy and all traffic to orders-api stops
After 45 seconds of continuous failed health checks, the ALB stops routing new requests to just that one target while the other two keep serving traffic normally
The ALB automatically restarts the failing container itself
Nothing happens until a human manually deregisters the target

prompt: A target-tracking auto-scaling policy uses ALBRequestCountPerTarget with target_value = 1000. What does this policy actually do when traffic rises?
choices: It restarts all existing tasks to free up memory
It adds enough tasks to bring the average per-target request rate back down near 1000 requests/minute, rather than always adding exactly one task
It immediately scales to max_capacity regardless of how much traffic increased
It lowers the ALB's health check interval to detect failures faster

prompt: Why does the auto-scaling policy use a longer scale_in_cooldown (120s) than scale_out_cooldown (60s)?
choices: AWS requires scale_in_cooldown to always be exactly double scale_out_cooldown
Scaling in is technically slower to execute than scaling out
To avoid thrashing: reacting fast to real load increases is useful, but removing capacity too quickly after a brief traffic dip risks needing it again moments later
Shorter cooldowns on scale-in reduce AWS billing costs

prompt: A Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler is configured with averageUtilization: 70 on the cpu resource, for a service whose actual bottleneck is database connection pool exhaustion under concurrent load, not CPU cycles. What's the problem with this setup?
choices: HPA cannot use CPU as a metric at all
CPU utilization is a weak proxy for this service's real bottleneck, so the HPA may fail to scale out before the service degrades even though CPU looks fine
minReplicas and maxReplicas cannot both be set in the same HPA
HorizontalPodAutoscaler only works with Deployments, never with services under load

prompt: A team deploys orders-api's containers to both us-east-1 and eu-west-1, each pointed at its own independent writable Postgres primary, and calls it done. What's the real problem with this specific setup?
choices: Nothing — two independent writable primaries in two regions is a complete, production-ready multi-region design
Two independent writable primaries for the same logical data can diverge with no conflict-resolution mechanism, risking silent data inconsistency between regions
ECS Fargate cannot run in more than one AWS region at all
Terraform cannot provision resources in two regions in the same configuration

prompt: In the Route 53 latency-based routing setup, what does evaluate_target_health = true actually accomplish?
choices: It makes DNS queries resolve faster by skipping health checks entirely

It ties routing to the same ALB target-group health checks from the load balancing section, so a region whose targets are all unhealthy is automatically excluded from DNS answers, enabling real regional failover
It forces all traffic to always go to us-east-1 regardless of latency

prompt: A customer in Frankfurt updates their shipping address (write goes to the us-east-1 primary), then immediately loads a confirmation page served from the eu-west-1 read replica and sees the old address. What does this demonstrate?
choices: A bug in the application's write logic that needs to be fixed
Cross-region read replicas introduce a real replication lag window during which reads in the replica's region can be stale relative to a very recent write elsewhere
Route 53 latency-based routing sent the write to the wrong region
The ALB health check for eu-west-1 is misconfigured
